Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

Eileen Myles' poem "Peanut Butter" (or this untitled work) depicts a woman standing alone in her bright kitchen late at night, smoking her final cigarette of "smoking youth" and sweetening an odd cup of tea as she approaches the milestone of turning thirty. Through mundane sensory details—Billie Holiday on the radio, honey dripping down a plastic bear's face like tears—the poem captures a quiet, melancholic moment of self-reflection and aging, transforming ordinary domestic solitude into a poignant meditation on the passage of time.

Keywords: Billie, Holiday, Ivy

outputs.L1:
Billie Holiday drifted from the radio as I stood in the kitchen, smoking a cigarette from the pack I intended to finish tonight—my last night of youthful smoking. I had brewed a cup of some peculiar tea that had been lingering in my cupboard. It was a little too sweet, an odd blend, yet my only impulse was to make it sweeter still.

Ivy Anderson was singing, and the hour had grown late in my brightly lit kitchen. I stood beside the tub, feeling somewhat older—nearly thirty—in that luminous kitchen tonight. I am not an unattractive woman, I suppose. Oh, how quiet it is in my kitchen tonight. I squeezed the plastic honey bear, and a thin thread of honey drizzled into the strange, sweet tea.

It was quite late. The honey bear's cap had come loose, and somehow the honey trickled down the bear's face, pooling in the crevices beneath its eyes—oh, so sad and sweet. I stood there in my kitchen. Oh, honey, I found myself gazing at the honey bear's face.
outputs.L2: The sounds of Billie Holiday drifted from the radio while I lingered in the kitchen, drawing on a cigarette from the pack I intend to empty before the night ends—my final night as a smoker of my youth. I brewed myself a strange sort of tea that had been sitting around untouched. The flavor was slightly too sweet, a peculiar blend. Yet the only urge I had was to add even more sweetness. Ivy Anderson's voice filled the space quite late this evening, here in my brilliantly lit kitchen. I lean against the tub, sensing the weight of age, almost thirty years old now, beneath these bright lights tonight. I'd say I'm not unattractive, really. How still everything feels in my kitchen this evening as I press on this plastic honey bear, watching a thin strand of honey trickle into that oddly sweet tea. The hour has grown late. The bear's lid wasn't fastened properly, so honey somehow ran down across its face, pooling in the little grooves under its eyes—so mournful and sweet at once. Here I stand in my kitchen, oh honey, my gaze fixed on the honey bear's face.
outputs.L3:
On the radio, late at night, Billie Holiday and Ivy Anderson trade their sorrows back and forth, their voices threading through the static while I sit smoking in the hard, bright light of the kitchen. Everything here is illuminated—the white counters, the chrome faucet, the small blue flame beneath the kettle—as if the room itself refuses to let anything hide in shadow.

This is the last night, I've decided, the final night of my smoking youth. Tomorrow I will be someone else, someone who does not do this, but tonight I intend to finish the entire pack, one cigarette after another, until there is nothing left but the crumpled cellophane and the smell of it in my hair. There is a strange ceremony in it, this deliberate ending.

I've made myself a cup of tea to go with the smoke, though it has turned into something odd, far too sweet, more syrup than tea. And yet I feel compelled only to make it sweeter still, tipping the plastic honey bear over the cup and watching the amber ribbon fall, as though sweetness were the only thing that could balance whatever else the night holds.

Standing here by the tub, nearly thirty years old now, I catch myself thinking about age, about the way time moves through a body without asking permission. I am not a bad looking woman. I say it plainly, without vanity—it is simply true, and there is a small comfort in knowing it, in facing the mirror and the years without flinching.

The honey keeps dripping down the little bear's face, gathering and catching just beneath its eyes, and something about this strikes me as unbearably sad and sweet all at once—those two golden tears that will not fall, held there in the bright kitchen light while the women on the radio go on singing about everything we lose.
outputs.L4:
# Peanut Butter: A Meditation on Time and Solitude

In Eileen Myles' evocative poem "Peanut Butter," an ordinary moment becomes a canvas for profound reflection. The scene is deceptively simple: a woman stands alone in her brightly lit kitchen during the small hours of the night. The harsh clarity of the kitchen light contrasts with the darkness pressing against the windows, creating an atmosphere of isolation that is somehow both intimate and stark. She is not doing anything remarkable—just standing, present in her own space, wrapped in the particular quiet that only the deepest hours of night can offer.

The cigarette she smokes carries unexpected weight. It is, as she thinks of it, the last cigarette of her "smoking youth"—a phrase that transforms a mundane habit into a marker of a life stage soon to end. She stands on the threshold of turning thirty, that milestone which carries such cultural and personal significance, the age at which youth is conventionally understood to give way to something more settled, more serious, more adult. Each inhalation becomes a small ritual, a goodbye to the person she has been, the freedoms and carelessness of her twenties dissolving into smoke.

Around her, the domestic details accumulate with quiet significance. Billie Holiday's voice drifts from the radio, her melancholic phrasing filling the empty kitchen with a companionable sadness—the perfect soundtrack to solitary late-night contemplation. On the counter sits a plastic honey bear, that familiar and slightly absurd container found in countless kitchens. As she sweetens her cup of tea, honey drips down the bear's face, and in this small observation the poem finds its emotional core: the honey resembles tears streaming down the bear's cheeks.

This image—honey as tears—captures the entire tenor of the moment. It is at once faintly comic and deeply poignant, finding in the most trivial object a reflection of her own unspoken emotion. The bear weeps sweetness, just as she stands weeping in her own quiet, unshed way at the passage of time. The "odd cup of tea" she prepares suggests something out of the ordinary, a comfort sought at an unusual hour, a small gesture of self-care amid the loneliness.

What makes the poem so affecting is precisely its restraint. Myles does not editorialize or announce the significance of the scene. Instead, she trusts the sensory details—the light, the smoke, the music, the honey—to convey the weight of the moment. The genius of the poem lies in this transformation: an entirely ordinary experience, one that millions of people might have on any given night, becomes a meditation on aging, on the quiet grief of leaving one part of life behind, and on the strange beauty of standing alone with one's own consciousness.

Ultimately, "Peanut Butter" celebrates and mourns in equal measure. It honors the small, unglamorous moments that make up a life while acknowledging the melancholy that attends the awareness of time slipping away. In the woman's solitary kitchen vigil, Myles finds something universal: the human confrontation with change, the tender ache of thresholds crossed, and the way that even a dripping honey bear can, in the right light and the right silence, break the heart.

# The Voice That Climbed Like Ivy

Billie Holiday remains one of the most unforgettable voices in the history of jazz. Born Eleanora Fagan in 1915, she rose from a difficult childhood to become one of the most influential singers of the twentieth century. Her music carried a raw emotional honesty that few artists have ever matched, turning every lyric into a deeply personal confession.

What set Billie apart was not technical perfection but feeling. Her phrasing bent and stretched like a melody all its own, and she could transform even the simplest song into something haunting. Classics such as "Strange Fruit," "God Bless the Child," and "Lady Sings the Blues" showcased her ability to blend beauty with sorrow.

Much like ivy, her influence spread quietly but persistently, climbing across the walls of music history and taking root in the styles of countless artists who followed. Singers from Frank Sinatra to modern jazz vocalists have credited her with shaping the way they approach a song. Her legacy clung to the culture and refused to fade, growing stronger with each passing decade.

Billie Holiday's life was marked by hardship, including struggles with addiction and racial injustice, yet her artistry never dimmed. Even during her final holiday seasons—when her health had begun to fail—she poured everything she had into her performances, giving audiences moments of unguarded truth.

Today, listening to Billie Holiday feels like discovering something timeless. Her recordings continue to comfort, challenge, and inspire, a reminder that true artistry, like ivy, endures long after the season has passed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in stream-of-consciousness style about a woman alone in her kitchen late at night, the night before she quits smoking, turning thirty.
counterfactuals.output:
The Last Night of Twenties

The clock says 11:47 and the pack has three left, three little soldiers standing in their crushed paper barracks, and I keep telling myself just one more, just this one, the way I've told myself just one more for eleven years now since I was nineteen and stole them from my mother's purse thinking I was so grown, so sophisticated, exhaling into the parking lot behind the diner where I worked and thought that job was temporary too.

The kitchen tile is cold under my bare feet and the refrigerator hums its one long note, the note it's always humming, the note I never hear until nights like this when the house goes quiet enough to hear myself think and thinking is exactly what I don't want to do.

Thirty. In twelve minutes and change. Thirty like a door closing, thirty like my mother at thirty already had me and a mortgage and lines around her mouth from pulling on these same white sticks, and here I am with a lease and a plant I keep almost killing and a phone that isn't ringing.

I light one anyway. Of course I do. The flame, the pull, the small red eye of it glowing in the dark window where my reflection sits looking back at me, some woman I half-recognize, hair down, robe open, holding the last of something.

They say your cells replace themselves, that in seven years you're entirely new, not a single piece of the girl in the diner parking lot left in this body, and if that's true then who has been smoking all this time, who made all these promises, who is the one who keeps breaking them, and the smoke curls up past the light fixture with the dead bug in it I keep meaning to clean and I think maybe tomorrow, maybe tomorrow I'll be someone who cleans the light fixtures, someone who doesn't do this, someone whose lungs are pink again and whose fingers don't smell like this and whose thirties are the good decade, the decade where it all comes together, the decade I've been waiting for during all the decades that were supposed to be practice.

Two left now.

The ashtray was my grandmother's, cut glass, heavy, and she smoked until the day the doctor showed her the x-ray and even then she'd sneak them and I loved her for that weakness more than for any strength she ever had, loved the human smallness of her wanting, and I press the ember out and watch it die and think that wanting is the thing, isn't it, the wanting is what I'm really quitting, learning to sit in a kitchen at midnight and want nothing, need nothing, just be a woman and a hum and a cold floor and the turning over of a year.

11:58.

I could save the last two. Keep them. A test. Or I could smoke them both right now, back to back, a farewell, a going-out-in-glory, and tomorrow throw the empty pack away like a body I'm done living in.

The window shows me the woman again. She looks tired. She looks like she might make it. She looks thirty, or close enough to reach out and touch it, and I raise my hand and she raises hers and for a second we are the same, the girl and the woman and the smoke and the years, all of us here in the kitchen, all of us deciding, and the clock rolls over quiet as a held breath and it is done, the day arrives the way all days do, without ceremony, without asking, and there are two cigarettes left and a whole life I haven't smoked yet and I stand very still and let the humming fill me up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece in the style of Eileen Myles about a small domestic moment involving honey, tea, and Billie Holiday on the radio.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Honey**

I am standing
in the kitchen
which is really
just the corner
of the room
where the light
gives up
and Billie is on
the radio doing
that thing
she does
where she waits
a half second
too long
to arrive
at the word
and you forgive
her
you always
forgive her
because she came
anyway.
The kettle.
I don't want
to talk about
the kettle
except it's
the loudest
thing
I own
and then it isn't.
I put the honey in
the tea
and the honey
does that
slow disappearing
which is not
disappearing
it's just
becoming
the tea
and I think
that's probably
the nicest
thing
that can happen
to a person
if you're lucky
if you get
the right cup.
I don't have
a lot
to report.
The spoon
is warm now.
Billie is telling me
about somebody
who did her wrong
and she sounds
so good about it
so completely
alright
about the wrong
that I stand here
holding
my little heat
in both hands
not drinking it
yet
just holding it
letting the morning
be a thing
that isn't
asking me
for anything.
The honey
is gone.
It's in there.
I mean
it's fine.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person free-verse poem where a nearly-thirty woman smokes her last cigarette and notices honey dripping down a plastic honey bear's face.
counterfactuals.output:
**Last One**

I am twenty-nine and eleven months,
which is to say I am almost something
I haven't decided how to feel about.

The kitchen is doing that gray thing it does
before the light commits to morning,
and I am smoking on the counter
by the open window like a girl,
though girlhood left without saying goodbye,
the way people do at parties
you didn't want to be at anyway.

Last one. I mean it this time.
I've meant it before—
the way you mean things
when meaning them is free.

On the shelf the honey bear is weeping.
Someone (me) left the cap loose,
and a slow amber tear
is working its way down the plastic snout,
catching the almost-light,
going gold at the throat.

It moves the way honey moves,
which is to say the way I move
toward thirty—
not slow exactly,
just certain,
just downward and sweet
and impossible to catch
once it starts.

I could wipe it. I don't.
There's something in me
that wants to watch a thing
finish what it's doing,
even the small dumb tragedy
of a bear that can't stop giving
what was put inside it.

The cigarette goes out between my fingers.
The honey reaches the shelf
and pools, and holds,
and shines like it has all the time
in the world—

which, unlike me,
it does.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a melancholy, run-on interior monologue set in a very bright kitchen late at night, with jazz playing and small sensory details.
counterfactuals.output: The refrigerator hums its one endless note under the jazz, the trumpet on the little speaker bending blue around the corners of the room, and here I am at almost two in the morning under lights so bright they feel like an accusation, everything too white, the counter gleaming, the tile gleaming, my own hands looking foreign and pale spread out on the formica like something I found rather than something I own, and there's the tea going cold in the mug I keep meaning to throw out because it's chipped at the lip and I always feel the crack against my mouth, small betrayal, and the saxophone comes in now, slow, the way somebody enters a room when they already know you're not going to be happy to see them, and I keep thinking about how you used to stand right here, right where the light pools on the floor, and how you'd sway a little when this kind of music played, barely moving, more like the idea of dancing than the dancing itself, and the honey jar has crystallized into a solid amber block I can't get the spoon through, and outside the window it's just my reflection floating in the dark, kitchen twin, watching me with that same worn-out look, and the linoleum is cold through my socks, and somewhere a pipe ticks as it cools, and the jazz keeps unspooling like it has somewhere to be even though none of us do, not me, not the moth batting itself against the bulb, not the dishes I've stopped pretending I'll wash tonight, and I think the loneliest hour isn't the dark one, it's this one, this fluorescent brightness with nowhere to hide a single shadow, no soft corner to fold yourself into, just the hum and the horn and the cold tea and the long white light going on and on like it's forgotten how to stop.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about aging, loneliness, and sweetness using imagery of an odd cup of tea and a honey bear bottle.
counterfactuals.output:
# Honey Bear at Midnight

The kettle's whistle is the only voice
that answers me these evenings now,
and steam rises like the ghost of company
in a kitchen grown too quiet.

I take down the odd cup—
the one with the hairline crack,
chipped at the lip, its painted roses
faded soft as memory,
the mismatched saucer lost to years.
It fits my hand the way old things do,
worn to the shape of holding.

And there he stands, my little sentinel,
the honey bear, translucent gold,
his belly thinner than it used to be,
his shoulders squeezed to sweetness
season after season.
I turn him upside down and wait—
patience is a thing you learn
when you have only time.

The amber drips, unhurried, thick,
a slow gold thread let down
into the dark well of the tea,
dissolving, warming,
turning bitterness to something
I can swallow.

There is a kindness in this ritual:
the crack that never spilled,
the bear who gives until he's empty,
the tea that meets me halfway
between the day and sleep.

I am old. The house is large with silence.
But sweetness keeps.
It waits in cupboards, sticky-lidded, faithful,
and every cup I pour is proof
that something bitter,
gently tended,
can still be made to taste like grace.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
